parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”). Doublet of eslavo, esloveno, esclavão /eslavão, and tchau /chau.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin Slavus, from Sclavus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more. Doublet of escravo, esloveno, esclavão /eslavão, and tchau /chau.

parole.significato: to stigmatize (to characterize as disgraceful or ignominious)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stigmatizō.
From Latin Melchita, from Byzantine Greek Μελχίτης (Melkhítēs), from Classical Syriac ܡܠܟܝܐ (malkāyāʾ, “royal; royalist”) + Byzantine Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). See these for more.

parole.significato: metaphysics (branch of philosophy that studies first principles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin metaphysica, methephisica, from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσικά (metaphusiká). See English metaphysics for further etymology.

parole.significato: metaphysician (philosopher who specializes in the scholarly study of metaphysics)
parole.testo: From metafísica (“metaphysics”), from Medieval Latin metaphysica (“metaphysics”), from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσικά (metaphusiká). By surface analysis, meta- + físico.
From Latin opalus, from Byzantine Greek ὀπάλλιος (opállios), from Sanskrit उपल (upala, “gem, stone”).

parole.significato: patriarch (male head of a community or household)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese patriarca, patriarcha, borrowed from Late Latin patriarcha, from Byzantine Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “-arch”).

parole.significato: to systematize (to arrange into a systematic order)
parole.testo: From sistemático (via Late Latin from Byzantine Greek συστηματικός (sustēmatikós), from σύστημα (sústēma, “organised whole, body”)) + -izar. By surface analysis, sistema + -izar.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese turquo, from Medieval Latin Turcus, borrowed from Byzantine Greek Τοῦρκος (Toûrkos), borrowed from Classical Persian ترک, from Old Turkic 𐱅𐰇𐰼𐰜 (t²ẅr²ẅk²), from Proto-Turkic *tür(ü)k.

parole.significato: varnish (type of paint that leaves a hard, glossy film)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese verniz, a borrowing from Medieval Latin vernīcem (“varnish”) < veronīx, from Byzantine Greek, from Ancient Greek Βερενίκη (Bereníkē, “a city in Lybia”).
